because the Bible doesn't say anything at all. It can't. It does not speak. It is not a sensient agent. It can neither
speak nor clarify nor correct nor elaborate. It is a text and texts do not have inherent meaning. Meaning is
generated in the mind of a reader, a hearer or a viewer when they engage the
text in a set of social and historical circumstances. And because readers,
hearers, and viewers are different and social and historical circumstances are different, we generate many different
sets of meaning. But even that's reductive because the Bible is not a text. It's a collection of texts written
by many different people in many different times, places, and circumstances to many different audiences for many different reasons.
And when we do our best to try to understand what we think the authors and editors were trying to communicate to
their audiences within their own sets of social and historical circumstances,
what we end up with is a lot of contradictory things. In other words, to the degree that the Bible says anything
at all, it says a lot of contradictory things. So the Bible says so is
meaningless. The Bible says nothing. We say so with the Bible as our proof text.
And what we say is really mostly dependent on what we want to say or what we need to say. And I can demonstrate
this because if I were to ask if it is a sin to eat food that has been sacrificed
to an idol, I'm going to get different responses throughout the entire Hebrew Bible. That's a big time no. And even in
Acts 15, the Jerusalem council after they determined that gentile converts to following Jesus didn't have to obey the
law of Moses, they did say, "But there are four things that you have to obey.
You have to abstain from sexual immorality, from eating things sacrificed to idols, from things strangled, and from blood."
So, they got rid of the entire law of Moses except for four things. And three of those things were dietary restrictions. But if we go to Romans,
Paul says that doesn't matter. That's not a sin. Unless you're doing it in the presence of a weaker follower of Jesus
who does not know that an idol is nothing in the world. And doing so might scandalize that weaker Christian. Then it becomes a sin to eat something that
has been sacrificed to an idol. But otherwise, nah. And Christians today have overwhelmingly, not unilaterally,
but overwhelmingly rejected any kinds of dietary restrictions. Meaning, they have rejected
75% of what the Jerusalem Council decided were the only rules that followers of Jesus still had to follow
from the law of Moses. So, what does the Bible say? A bunch of different stuff.
And what of it do we honor today regarding eating food sacrificed to idols? None of it. Because it doesn't
matter what the Bible says. It only matters what we say. But when we want what we say to be inherent and inspired
and univocal and authoritative, we appeal to the Bible as the proof text.
We appeal to the Bible in order to baptize our opinion in order to endow it with God's authority. The same is true of slavery.
There's not a single syllable of the Bible that identifies the practice of buying, selling, and owning other human
beings as a sin. But we so identify it today. Why? Because we decided so. We
overruled the Bible on that. And then we went through and we negotiated with the text. We found passages that we could
identify as these secret little seeds that God was planting that wouldn't come to fruition for 1500 years cuz God was
slow playing their hand on this one. And it just coincidentally wouldn't happen until we
recovered Greek philosophy and we had the Renaissance and the Reformation and then the Enlightenment and we suddenly realized that all these things that
Greek philosophy said were important are now important again. And we
negotiated an opposition to slavery into the Bible because again the Bible is not the authority. The Bible is just words
on a page. We endow them with meaning and we endow them with authority. So the reality is that our opinion is what
matters. And the Bible doesn't say anything at all. It only speaks to the degree we inject it with our opinions.
